title: What If Your Moon Jump Went Too High?
topic: What if your Moon jump went too high? (Apollo 16, Charlie Duke's 1972 fall onto his life-support backpack)
mechanism: The Moon cuts your weight to about a sixth but not your mass: a big push sends a suited astronaut four feet up, and once the heavy life-support backpack starts tipping him backward it keeps going, so Charlie Duke landed on the fiberglass shell that held his air.

beats.hook: On the Moon a four-foot jump nearly killed a man, and his own backpack did it: Duke rising past the flag, his shocked face in the helmet, the backpack slamming into the dust.
beats.but: April 1972, Apollo 16: Duke and Young finish their last moonwalk; Munich's Olympics are coming, so they invent the Moon Olympics.
beats.then: Young shows off, jumping flat-footed straight up and bouncing like a kid in one-sixth gravity; Duke wants to beat him and flies about four feet high.
beats.conflict: As he straightens up the backpack pulls him over backward, he can't correct it, and falls four feet right onto the backpack: that backpack is his air. Houston flinches.
beats.pivot: You see, the Moon cuts your weight but not your mass: the pack weighed as much as Duke, so once it tips it keeps going; and it is a fiberglass shell, crack it and the air rushes out.
beats.so: Young: 'Charlie! That ain't very smart.' He helps him up; Duke freezes, listening for a hiss; nothing, the pack held. Now picture you, jumping twice as high, flipping right over. That's why moonwalkers loped and skipped.
beats.closing: So on the Moon, keep your jumps small. Remember the man who didn't. (hands over to: On the Moon, a jump of just four feet nearly killed a man...)

triple_hook.visual: Charlie Duke in his white suit is already rising past the striped flag in front of the gold-foil lander, tipping back, black sky and the blue Earth behind, camera pushing up with him.
triple_hook.verbal: On the Moon, a jump of just four feet nearly killed a man, and his own backpack did it.
triple_hook.text: WHAT IF YOU JUMP TOO HIGH?

seed.what: Duke's big white life-support backpack (PLSS), on screen from the first beat, the thing that tips him over and the shell that holds his air

characters.look: Charlie Duke, Apollo 16 lunar module pilot: 1972 A7LB white moon suit with no stripes, white lunar boots, white gloves, clear bubble helmet under the white visor assembly with the gold visor raised, big white life-support backpack (PLSS) with the small oxygen pack on top, dark hair
John Young, Apollo 16 commander: same 1972 white moon suit, backpack and helmet with commander's red stripes on the arms, legs and helmet, white lunar boots, dark hair
Tony England, CapCom in Houston 1972: short-sleeved white shirt, narrow dark tie, dark slacks, black shoes, headset with boom mic, short hair
A flight controller, Houston 1972: short-sleeved pale blue shirt, wide patterned tie, horn-rimmed glasses, headset, coffee mug
A 1972 high jumper in Munich: red sleeveless athletics vest, short shorts (1972 track kit), white running spikes
The viewer as an astronaut in a dream: white moon suit with orange accent stripes, helmet with a clear visor, backpack

gags.what: Young bounces like a kid: three boing hops, each kicking up clean ballistic dust arcs; the last hop's dust rains onto Duke's visor and he wipes it with a glove
Duke lands flat on his backpack, boots in the air, a ballistic dust ring sprays out and falls straight back down
In Houston, the controller flinches at the TV and his coffee mug tips over the console
The dream 'you' flips over twice like a pinwheel and lands head-first, stuck in the dust like a dart, legs kicking

props.prop: a giant dial scale labelled WEIGHT whose needle swings from EARTH down to 1/6
a heavy pack on a tipping post labelled MASS that tips and keeps going
the backpack cut open on a stand: FIBERGLASS shell, OXYGEN tank, a spreading crack and a falling gauge

format_note: The jump is staged at its sourced height of about four feet (1.2 m) on the puppet's 1.3 m scale; hang time is slowed for readability. The Earth is drawn larger in the sky than it would look from the Moon.
story_numbers: 1/6 on the scale dial (one sixth, sourced)
